chapter_theme: In the middle of her debate with the Sankhya teacher Neelakesi attacks his chain of principles: she asks whether mahat comes from prakriti, mocks the count of eleven organs and the organs of action, sets out the Jain view that the four elements are built of atoms and that space is one formless thing reaching beyond the world, denies that sound belongs to space, and argues that an unchanging soul and an unknowing nature can neither join anew nor produce anything.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Sankhya teacher at Hastinapura whom Neelakesi debates in this sarukkam (named சாங்கியன் in 730)

749.reading: Neelakesi takes the Sankhya's mahat, the principle said to give birth to the pride of 'I' and 'mine', and argues that whatever brings a thought into being must be a sentient thing, which her opponent never considered.
749.nuance: The Sankhya puts mahat on the side of unconscious nature; the objection turns that against him: producing the sense of self is a work of thought, and thought belongs to the sentient. The reading of சேதனை twice (lines 2 and 3) as the sentient is mine and the lines are compressed.

claims.claim: mahat is what gives rise to the sense of 'I' and 'mine'
only a sentient thing can bring a thought into being

750.reading: She asks whether mahat comes forth from prakriti or is a separate thing in its own right, says there is no third possibility, and bids him answer so that the learned may judge.
750.nuance: A dilemma: each horn is answered in the verses that follow (751 and 761). சான்றார் appeals to the assembly of the wise who judge a debate.

claims.claim: mahat comes forth from prakriti

751.reading: She presses the dilemma: if the quality is the first substance itself, nothing new has come forth, and if it is other than it, a further thing exists; she, skilled in speaking on scripture, asks what he can say to this.
751.nuance: Line 2 (அதற்பிறி தென்னி னதுமனனு முண்டா) is hard to construe; the sense that a distinct product would be a new thing beside prakriti is my reading. சுதப்பொருள் (line 4) praises her command of scripture.

752.reading: Neelakesi says that if the formless, unmanifest cause can bring forth its opposite, the world with form, he may as well say that empty space by itself creates gross things, and calls his words incoherent.
752.nuance: A reductio: the Sankhya's unmanifest (அவ்வியத்தம்) is formless, and if formless can yield form, any formless thing, space included, could. In 759 she gives the Jain view of space as formless and producing nothing.

claims.claim: the formless unmanifest cause brings forth the world with form
what is formless cannot produce gross things with form

753.reading: She says prakriti made of mutually hostile qualities, and products in which one quality comes to exceed the others, destroy his own thesis and leave all his classes empty, so his doctrine is only laughable and she will not believe it.
753.nuance: பகைக்குணம் (line 1) names the three qualities as enemies of one another; the point is that opposed qualities cannot form one stable cause, and if a product comes by one exceeding the rest, the balanced cause is already lost.

claims.claim: prakriti is made of three opposed qualities, and its products appear when one exceeds the others

754.reading: Mocking the count of organs, she says he made five organs of knowing and five of action, ten and one more, yet left out an organ of madness, an organ of possession and an organ of punching.
754.nuance: The joke rests on the Sanskrit names புத்தேந்திரியம் and கம்மேந்திரியம்: if every power of acting counts as an organ, there is no end to the list. The 'one' added to the ten is the mind.

claims.claim: there are five organs of knowing, five of action and the mind, eleven in all

755.reading: She turns to the five subtle elements that he says arise in between, and says that if he counts thought and the rest as qualities of the soul, not even Indra could match him.
755.nuance: The sarcasm of line 4 suggests that counting thought as the soul's quality would give away the Sankhya case, for which thought belongs to nature, and take the Jain side. Lines 1 and 2 (தந்திர மாவன ... வந்தர வாத்துவன்) are obscure and the reading of தந்திரம் as the subtle elements is a guess.

claims.claim: five subtle elements arise between the principle of self and the gross elements

756.reading: She asks: if hands, feet, the two organs of excretion and speech are organs, then let him show, having understood it, what sense object they act on and what knowledge they know.
756.nuance: A sense organ, for her, is defined by an object and a knowing; the five organs of action have neither, so calling them organs is a misuse of the word.

claims.claim: hands, feet, the two excretory organs and speech are organs
an organ is that which has an object and a knowledge of it

757.reading: If he says they are counted as organs because they act, she asks what fault there would be in adding the suckling breast, the lips, the eyebrows, the moving cheeks, the chewing teeth and the throat.
757.nuance: The reply to a defence the opponent might give (acting, கருமம்): the criterion of action would make every working part of the body an organ.

claims.claim: the organs of action are counted as organs because they act

758.reading: She sets out the Jain account: the five subtle qualities, smell and the rest, belong to matter bound up in atoms; they are what the senses grasp, and as atoms come together and grow in order they make the four kinds of elements, as reason shows.
758.nuance: Against the Sankhya's five elements unfolding from subtle elements, she counts four elements built of atoms, with smell and the other qualities as their sensed properties; space is kept apart and treated in 759. The construal of lines 1 and 4 is mine.

claims.claim: the four elements are built up from atoms, and smell and the other sense qualities belong to them

759.reading: Space, says the lady of beautiful long eyes, is one, extends through this world and the non-world beyond it, and is non-sentient and without form.
759.nuance: உலகு and அலோகம் (line 1) are the Jain world and non-world: space alone runs on beyond the world into the empty non-world, which is why space cannot be one of the elements that unfold from prakriti.

claims.claim: space is one, formless and non-sentient, and extends through the world and the non-world

760.reading: She says sound has form and so cannot rest in space, which is formless; in making sound belong to space he spoke against true teaching, says she of the deer-like gaze.
760.nuance: In the Jain view sound is matter, and so it has form; the Sankhya derives ear and sound from space. The epithet of line 4 is read as மான் மருவா வந்த நோக்கு, a gaze that came as a deer's.

claims.claim: sound belongs to space
sound has form and so cannot belong to formless space

761.reading: She sums up: mahat does not come from prakriti, nor the next principle from mahat; the many qualities that would compose them have no arising, and since the elements gain no reality, his principles are unfit.
761.nuance: This answers the dilemma of 750 by denying both horns: the chain of principles fails at its first link. அத்த (line 4) addresses the opponent as master, likely with irony.

claims.claim: the principles unfold in a chain from prakriti through mahat to the elements

762.reading: She says that if he joins the blind man and the lame man together to explain how soul and nature combine, the comparison does not make it clear, for those two act by their own understanding, while here the work is said to happen with no knower in it.
762.nuance: The blind man carrying the lame is the Sankhya's own image for nature that acts without seeing and the soul that sees without acting. Her objection, as I read lines 3 and 4, is that both men in the image are conscious and agree, which nature cannot do. The lines are terse and the reading is not secure.

claims.claim: soul and nature combine like a lame man riding a blind one, the one seeing and the other acting

763.reading: She asks what good it does to set out these classes of principles for a soul that never changes in any way, and says that if the comparison is pressed truly, his thesis and every part of his proof collapse.
763.nuance: If the soul is wholly unchanging (விகாரம் இலா), knowing the principles cannot change its state, so the teaching of the twenty-five loses its purpose; மேற்கோள் is the thesis of a formal proof.

claims.claim: the soul is without any change
teaching the principles can do nothing for a soul that cannot change

764.reading: Laughing, the lady of fair brow tells him to look and see: the soul and prakriti he praised, being of a kind that cannot produce even when joined, are like eunuchs who bear no child however they consort.
764.nuance: The image answers the Sankhya union of soul and nature: one does not act and the other does not know, so their joining yields nothing. Line 1 (குணத்தின் நீயவட்) is unclear; அவள் may be prakriti spoken of as female.

claims.claim: the world comes forth from the union of soul and prakriti
two things that can neither act and know together cannot produce by joining

765.reading: She argues that if soul and nature were joined everywhere even before, calling their union new means nothing, and the many things to be produced would have existed before as well.
765.nuance: Both soul and nature are said to pervade all, so they were never apart, and a first union that starts the world cannot happen; and if effects already exist in their cause, nothing is newly produced. The opening இல்லுளி is obscure.

claims.claim: the world begins when soul and nature come together
effects exist in their cause before they appear

links.note: In 516 Neelakesi tells the Buddha that sound travels until it reaches the ear; in 760 she tells the Sankhya that sound has form and so cannot belong to space.
links.teaches: The same Jain premise, that sound is matter, does the work against two opponents: it makes sound travel against the Buddhist and keeps it out of formless space against the Sankhya.

links.note: 295 says that without dharma and adharma the room of souls and matter would spill past the world's edge; 759 says space itself runs on through the world into the non-world.
links.teaches: Read together, the two verses show why the Jain account needs a limit beyond space: space has no edge, so the world's bound must come from the conditions of motion and rest.

links.note: In 736 the Sankhya says the soul does nothing, has no quality, is eternal and present everywhere; in 765 Neelakesi uses that all-presence to deny that soul and nature ever newly join.
links.teaches: The opponent's own praise of the soul as everywhere present becomes the premise that undoes his account of creation by union, since a thing never absent cannot newly arrive.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain speaker says space gives room to all things; Neelakesi says space is one, formless, non-sentient and extends through world and non-world.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic's report of Jain space matches the Jain epic's own voice on its function, while only the Neelakesi adds the non-world beyond the world, the part an outside report left out.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker derives the ear and sound from space (line 214); 760 says sound has form and cannot belong to formless space.
links.teaches: The derivation the Buddhist epic lets the Sankhya state unanswered is the very step the Jain epic attacks, so the two polemics differ less in what they report of Sankhya than in what they choose to contest.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker counts speech, hands, feet and the two excretory organs among the twenty-five principles; 756 denies these are organs, since they have no object and no knowing.
links.teaches: Set beside the plain Sankhya list in the Manimekalai, Neelakesi's mockery shows exactly which item of the count she treats as weakest: the organs of action, which fail her test that an organ must know something.

gains.a: The Neelakesi verse gains a case where the twenty-five lower principles are in fact used as a path to release, which is the use its objection says is impossible.
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a pointed objection it must meet: that seeing through the principles changes nothing if the soul who sees is unchangeable.

links.note: Tirumular says the soul reaches the saving state by seeing through the twenty-five principles, prakriti and maya; 763 says listing the principles can do nothing for a soul that never changes.
links.teaches: The pair shows what the Saiva use of the twenty-five needs and the Sankhya lacks: a soul that can be bound and freed, so that seeing through the principles is a real change of state.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (சாங்கிய வாதச் சருக்கம்); id as declared in neelakesi ch008, since vaadham is taken for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: a quality of a thing, lasting or passing, and its relation to the substance that bears it
new_concepts.label_source: as declared in neelakesi ch018; here குணம் (751), பகைக்குணம் and மிகைக்குணம் (753), பல்குணம் (761)

new_concepts.gloss: a sense faculty; in Jain teaching beings are graded by how many of the five senses they have
new_concepts.label_source: as declared in neelakesi ch004; here the verses use இந்திரியம் (754) and இந்தியம் (756)

source_issues: 761 line 1: the edition's '•' was repaired to ஃ (இஃதினு மஃதில்லை).
755 lines 1 and 2 (தந்திர மாவன ... வந்தர வாத்துவன்) are obscure and may be corrupt; the reading is a guess.
762 line 2 (பொருடம் தாக்கமும் போத்தந் துரைப்பிற்) has an odd word division and is hard to construe.
765 line 1 opens with இல்லுளி, which I cannot construe with confidence.
Chapter 33's span (730-748) lacks a verse 738 in the core file; noted here only as seen in the neighbouring show output.
